newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia coffee easier, supply increases.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia coffee easier, supply increases.

text.p: Indonesian Robusta coffee prices were easier on Monday, with supply increasing as farmhands worked overtime before heading to their hometowns to vote in the May 29 general election, traders said.

Grade four Robusta was quoted at 4,250-4,300 rupiah/kg in the key growing region of Lampung in South Sumatra, compared with 4,300-4,350 rupiah a week ago. The export price was quoted at $1,830-$1,850/tonne against $1,800-$1,850 last Monday.
"There's plenty of beans available at the moment," one trader said. "Workers have been busy harvesting before they leave for their villages to vote on Thursday."

"But demand has not been as hectic, but there are still buyers who are covering to fill contracts," the trader said. "Sellers are holding firm to their offer prices and are not keen on selling below the market range. If prices are not to their liking, they would rather hold on to their beans."
The traders said a holiday in Britain and the United States on Monday was keeping the market quiet, but added that local coffee prices were likely to stay steady through the week.
"I don't think prices will go down this week," one trader said. "Supply is likely to get tight after the general election because of a step-up in the harvest the past few days."
London coffee futures closed tightly mixed last Friday, with benchmark July rising $4 to close at $2,086 per tonne while September eased $2 to $2,098.
Traders said they expected the July contract to open unchanged to $20 lower when the market opens on Tuesday.
They also welcomed the Association of Coffee Producing Countries' (ACPC) decision last week to extend their export quotas for another 12 months, saying it would help prices.
"The export programme will help to keep prices stable after the current interest in coffee fades," one trader said. "But I think New York prices will ease because they are too high."
The 14-member ACPC reached an accord at a meeting in London last week to limit members' exports at 52.75 million bags for one year from July 1.
This compared with a cap for 1996/97 originally set at 53.55 million bags but later reduced by 800,000 bags.
